name: Zimbabwe
change_reason: v2: tier-2 page built from local, wire and think-tank sources
card_headline: Mnangagwa signed a law in July keeping himself in office to 2030 while critics face beatings and arrests, and ZiG inflation sits near 4 percent.
card_summary: President Emmerson Mnangagwa signed Constitutional Amendment No. 3 on 7 July 2026. It lengthens terms from five to seven years, moves the next election from 2028 to 2030 and has Parliament elect future presidents. [1] Rights groups document attacks and arrests of opponents. [2][3] Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga is the main rival inside ZANU-PF. [4] Annual ZiG inflation was 4.3 percent in October, but the government expects an El Nino drought to cut 2027 growth to 3.5 percent. [5][6]
card_local: New Zimbabwe reports the government calls the amendment irreversible while a Constitutional Court challenge awaits judgment. [7] ZimLive reports at least four court challenges to the Act. [8]
card_international: AFP and Reuters report the Senate vote of 75 to 4 and ZANU-PF's October decision to keep Mnangagwa as party leader past 2028. [9][10] Reuters reports the 19 November budget cutting 2027 growth to 3.5 percent. [6]
card_scholar: ISS analyst Peter Fabricius writes that Mnangagwa won the latest round against Chiwenga. [4] Brookings' Chipo Dendere calls the amendments a significant blow to anti-authoritarian efforts. [11] Afrobarometer found 79 percent backed the two-term limit in 2024. [12]
context_md: Mnangagwa came to power after a 2017 military coup ousted Robert Mugabe, who had ruled since independence in 1980. [9] The 2013 Constitution limited presidents to two five-year terms, which would have ended his rule in 2028. [1] He was elected in 2018 and re-elected in 2023, and ZANU-PF resolved in October 2025 to change the constitution to prolong presidential terms. [1] The opposition's 2023 gains in Parliament were reversed through recalls and by-elections that gave ZANU-PF a two-thirds majority. [11] Zimbabwe ranked 157th of 182 countries on Transparency International's 2025 corruption index. [11] The economy is on an IMF staff-monitored programme meant to build a track record toward arrears clearance. [13]

sections.title: The 2030 law is signed, and the courts have not stopped it
sections.body_md:
Mnangagwa signed the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 3) Act on 7 July 2026, after both houses of Parliament voted in June. [14][1] The National Assembly passed it 216 to 42 and the Senate followed on 24 June, 75 to 4. [9] The Act raises presidential and parliamentary terms from five to seven years, moves the next election from 2028 to 2030 and replaces the direct vote for president with election by Parliament. [1][15] ZimLive reports it was gazetted as Act No. 6 of 2026. [8]

The government's position, as New Zimbabwe reported on 26 October, is that the amendment is irreversible because it passed every legal stage, and that judges and senators appointed under the new framework are already sworn in. [7] No referendum was held. [16] Chipo Dendere of Wellesley College writes that the bill was fast-tracked to avoid one. [11] David Coltart, the Bulawayo mayor, argues a term extension would still need one, according to ISS. [4] This draft found no government statement explaining why none was held.

Court challenges have not worked so far. On 17 June the Constitutional Court dismissed two challenges filed before passage, one by six war veterans that it found flawed and one it said was not yet ready for decision. [17] On 18 July NCA member Vhurande Mahlupeko filed what ZimLive counts as at least the fourth challenge. He argues, among other grounds, that Parliament changed nine provisions that were not in the gazetted bill. [8] The respondents say the process is complete, and the court has reserved judgment on a related application. [7] Opposition figures say they will keep litigating. Tendai Biti said the law could signal a suspension of the constitution, and an MDC spokesperson said the party was preparing its own challenge. [18]

lenses.local: ZimLive and New Zimbabwe follow each filing; the government says the process is finished and the court has reserved judgment. [8][7]
lenses.international: AFP and Reuters carried the Senate vote, and critics quoted there call the change a "constitutional coup". [9] Human Rights Watch says international law sets no term length but requires genuine periodic elections. [1]
lenses.scholar: Dendere says the Constitutional Court dismissed challenges and left the opposition few routes to block the change. [11] Afrobarometer, as reported by New Zimbabwe, found 25 percent say Zimbabwe became less democratic in five years and 20 percent more. [19]

sections.title: The real contest is inside ZANU-PF: Chiwenga against Mnangagwa
sections.body_md:
First Vice-President Constantino Chiwenga, a retired general who helped lead the 2017 takeover, opposes the amendment, according to an analysis in The Standard. It describes the dispute as largely about succession and access to state resources. [20] The same piece reports that Mnangagwa demoted army chief Anselem Sanyatwe in March 2025, and that Justice Minister Ziyambi Ziyambi called a Chiwenga document alleging government corruption "palpably treasonous". [20] The page carries no byline, so this draft treats it as a single-sourced local account.

At ZANU-PF's annual conference in Chinhoyi in October, the party deferred its elective congress from 2027 to 2029, which keeps Mnangagwa as leader until 2030. New Zimbabwe says this aligns the party constitution with the amendment. [21] AFP reported that the party backed Mnangagwa, who is 84, to remain leader after 2028, and that one faction wants him in place to 2030 while another is positioning Chiwenga. [10]

Peter Fabricius of ISS wrote on 23 October that Chiwenga appeared to warn Mnangagwa against repeating 2017 and reportedly skipped events honouring him. Mnangagwa told unnamed rivals not to behave like "demons". [4] Coltart told ISS it is unclear how much army support Chiwenga keeps, because Mnangagwa has moved key figures away from the army. Hopewell Chin'ono argues Mnangagwa outmanoeuvred Chiwenga and that a coup is unlikely though not impossible, while Piers Pigou calls the rivalry a repeat contest between two factions. [4] Chiwenga's own account of the conference is not in this draft.

lenses.local: The Standard frames the split as a fight over succession and state resources. [20] New Zimbabwe reports the party congress moved to 2029. [21]
lenses.international: AFP says one party faction wants Mnangagwa to 2030 and another is positioning Chiwenga. [10]
lenses.scholar: ISS's Fabricius says Mnangagwa won the latest round; Coltart, Chin'ono and Pigou differ on how much the army still backs Chiwenga. [4]

sections.title: Opponents of the 2030 plan have been beaten and arrested, and a reporter has been charged
sections.body_md:
Human Rights Watch documented a run of attacks on opponents of the amendment. On 1 March 2026, about five to ten armed men in balaclavas entered the Harare offices of the National Constitutional Assembly and assaulted members, injuring leader Lovemore Madhuku. Madhuku told HRW the men said they were police, and police told HRW their officers "were not involved". [2] Amnesty International said the men beat people with batons in the presence of uniformed police. [22] On 5 March armed police were seen at the law offices of Tendai Biti, who leads the Constitutional Defenders Forum. Police said they were there to keep order and denied assault allegations. [2]

Students were also targeted. HRW recorded seven attacks on leaders of the Zimbabwe National Students Union, including abductions on 30 March, and said former union president Emmanuel Sitima and Takunda Mhuka were arrested on 14 April and denied bail. [3] CIVICUS rates civic space in Zimbabwe as Repressed. It reports that Biti and Morgan Ncube were arrested in Mutare on 21 March and bailed with conditions barring meetings without police approval, and that activist Godfrey Karembera was acquitted on 3 June after more than seven months in pre-trial detention. [15] The Zimbabwe Peace Project counted 145 violations affecting 3,675 people in April alone. [23]

The press is under pressure too. CPJ reported that Bulawayo24 reporter Gideon Madzikatidze had been detained since 18 February over a December story on a waste company, and faced cyberbullying and broadcasting charges. [24] CIVICUS reports journalists covering public hearings in Harare on 31 March were obstructed and some pressed to delete footage. [15] This draft did not find how the Madzikatidze case ended.

lenses.local: The Zimbabwe Peace Project, reported by 263Chat, counted 145 violations in April, and New Zimbabwe and ZimLive carry the court filings. [23]
lenses.international: HRW, Amnesty and CPJ each documented attacks, arrests or detentions between February and April. [2][22][24]
lenses.scholar: This draft found no academic or think-tank study of the 2026 crackdown beyond the Brookings commentary on the failed legal routes. [11]

sections.title: The ZiG has held and inflation is low, but a drought and arrears threaten the gains
sections.body_md:
The IMF approved a 10-month staff-monitored programme in 2026. It is not a lending programme and is meant to build a track record toward a Fund-supported one. [13] On 7 July IMF staff reached agreement on the first review. They reported real growth of 8.3 percent in 2025, projected about 5 percent for 2026, and said inflation had stayed low because of tight monetary conditions and relative exchange rate stability. [25] All quantitative targets were met, though one target on protected social and priority spending was missed. [25]

Zimstat's October figure for annual ZiG inflation was 4.3 percent, up from 3.7 percent in September. [5] The IMF says clearing external arrears and restoring debt sustainability are central to re-engagement. [25] In the 19 November budget, Finance Minister Mthuli Ncube targeted arrears clearance to the World Bank, African Development Bank and European Investment Bank by the end of March 2027. [6]

The next risk is climate. Zimbabwe expects an El Nino drought. Ncube said the budget would set aside $250 million in cash and $250 million for grain, and projected a 2027 maize harvest of 1.6 million tonnes, nearly 30 percent below 2026 and below the 2.2 million tonnes the country needs. [26] The government cut its 2027 growth forecast to 3.5 percent from 5 percent. [6] FEWS NET expected crisis-level food insecurity (IPC Phase 3) to appear from October in deficit areas, with fuel prices about 25 to 28 percent above their pre-February levels. It also counted over 115,000 returnees from South Africa through Beitbridge between late May and late July. [27]

lenses.local: New Zimbabwe reports Zimstat's 4.3 percent October inflation figure. [5]
lenses.international: Reuters reports the 2027 growth cut and the plan for a $500 million cash and grain reserve. [6][26]
lenses.scholar: The IMF credits tight policy and exchange rate stability for low inflation, and warns a strong El Nino could cut growth to 2 to 3 percent. [25]

sections.title: Land compensation is being paid slowly, and lithium and foreign deals run through China and Russia
sections.body_md:
Land reform entered a new phase in 2026. Al Jazeera reported on 13 August that 67 farms protected by bilateral investment agreements are being returned to investors from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Switzerland, and that 840 farms acquired "in error" are to go back to Black Zimbabwean owners. [28] A further 409 white farmers who stayed on the land may buy the portions they occupy. Agriculture Minister Anxious Masuka told Parliament this should not be mistaken for a return to the pre-reform era. [28] New Zimbabwe reported on 4 August that the government has paid $40 million to 93 farms with investment-treaty protection and owes $70.5 million, which it plans to cover in the 2027 and 2028 budgets. [29]

Lithium ties the economy to China. On 25 February the mines minister suspended exports of all raw minerals and lithium concentrate with immediate effect, citing malpractices in exports. Zimbabwe shipped 1.128 million tonnes of spodumene concentrate in the year to December 2025, mostly to China. [30] Semafor reports Zimbabwe produced almost 10 percent of world mined lithium last year, per the US Geological Survey, and that Chinese firms including Sichuan Yahua, Huayou and Sinomine are building lithium sulfate plants there. [31] On 25 June Ncube said Harare was in talks with China Railway on resource-linked financing and that the concentrate ban would take effect in January 2027 as planned. [32] How that squares with the February suspension is unclear in these sources.

Russia is a smaller but visible partner. The state-controlled Herald reported that Mnangagwa and Putin met in Moscow in May 2025, at least their fourth meeting, and named energy, space, mining and agriculture as cooperation areas without listing new agreements. [33] Mnangagwa led a delegation to the third Russia-Africa summit in Moscow in late October 2026, with talks with Putin scheduled. [34] The outcome of those talks was not found.

lenses.local: New Zimbabwe tracks compensation at $40 million paid and $70.5 million owed, and reported the Moscow summit delegation. [29][34]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, Reuters and Semafor cover the minerals ban and Chinese plants; AFP and Reuters report 22 heads of state at the Moscow summit. [30][31][35]
lenses.scholar: Brookings' Dendere says the export bans and local processing rules could give Western partners a way to press for transparency. [11]

timeline.text: Military-backed takeover ends Robert Mugabe's rule and Mnangagwa takes power.
Mnangagwa is re-elected after winning in 2018.
ZANU-PF resolves to change the constitution to prolong presidential terms.
The SAPES Trust offices in Harare are badly damaged in a suspected arson attack hours before a dialogue on the term extension.
The mines minister suspends exports of all raw minerals and lithium concentrate.
Armed men assault members at the National Constitutional Assembly offices in Harare, injuring Lovemore Madhuku.
Tendai Biti and Morgan Ncube are arrested in Mutare and bailed two days later with meeting restrictions.
The IMF approves a staff-monitored programme for Zimbabwe.
The Constitutional Court dismisses two challenges to the bill.
The Senate passes the bill 75 to 4, a week after the National Assembly voted 216 to 42.
Mnangagwa signs the amendment into law.
NCA member Vhurande Mahlupeko files a Constitutional Court application to void the Act.
Zimbabwe announces it will return 67 treaty-protected farms to investors and restore 840 farms to Black owners.
Finance Minister Ncube announces a $500 million cash and grain reserve against an El Nino drought.
ZANU-PF conference in Chinhoyi defers the elective congress to 2029 and keeps Mnangagwa as leader to 2030.
Mnangagwa leads a delegation to the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.
The 2027 budget cuts the growth forecast to 3.5 percent and targets arrears clearance to three lenders by March 2027.

factchecks.claim: Zimbabwe's currency is still in hyperinflation.
factchecks.by: A recurring framing in coverage that links today's ZiG to the Mugabe-era collapse; no single originator identified.
factchecks.evidence: Zimstat put annual ZiG inflation at 4.3 percent in October 2026, and the IMF projects an average of about 5.1 percent for 2026, crediting tight monetary conditions and relative exchange rate stability. The IMF still urges a tight stance until inflation expectations are firmly anchored.

factchecks.by: David Coltart, as reported by ISS, and applicants in Constitutional Court filings.

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters and AFP file on Zimbabwe at set points such as the Senate vote, the signing and the budget. [9][6] Day-to-day coverage of the repression and the court cases comes mostly from ZimLive, New Zimbabwe and NewsDay. [8][7] Think-tank output is steady but small, with ISS and Brookings pieces in June and October. [4][11]

severity.basis: There is no armed conflict, but HRW and Amnesty document armed men attacking opponents, and the Zimbabwe Peace Project counted 145 violations in April. [2][22][23]
FEWS NET expected crisis-level food insecurity in deficit areas from October, and the government projects a maize shortfall of about 600,000 tonnes in 2027. [27][26]
CIVICUS rates civic space Repressed, and the amendment ends direct presidential elections and extends terms to 2030. [15][1]
Inflation is 4.3 percent and growth was 8.3 percent in 2025, but external arrears are unresolved and 2027 growth is forecast to fall to 3.5 percent. [5][25][6]
Political space narrowed through 2026 as the amendment passed and ZANU-PF extended its leader's tenure, while the currency steadied under the IMF programme. [1][21][25]

parts.basis: Chinese firms are building lithium sulfate plants and China Railway is in talks on resource-linked financing, and Mnangagwa met Putin in May 2025 and went to the Moscow summit in October 2026. [31][32][33][34]
Zimbabwe produced almost 10 percent of world mined lithium in 2025. [31]
More than 115,000 returnees crossed from South Africa at Beitbridge in two months of 2026, and the ZANU-PF succession fight is described as the biggest near-term threat to stability. [27][20]
The main cross-border effect found in this draft is returnee movement from South Africa, and no source on the size of the diaspora was read. [27]
HRW says the amendment, passed amid repression, raises grave concerns, and Brookings argues it removes a check on one-person rule. [1][11]

summary: Zimbabwe scores mid-range because its lithium sector draws Chinese capital and its government courts Russia, while its borders carry a returnee flow rather than a refugee crisis. [31][33][27]
The precedent score reflects a parliamentary route around term limits that other incumbents may study, which this draft could not test against regional comparisons. [11]
gi.up: A contested succession in which the army and ZANU-PF factions split openly, or a mass return of migrants from South Africa.
gi.down: A settled succession and a negotiated debt deal that normalises Zimbabwe's ties with Western lenders.

gaps: Local sourcing is solid on politics, the courts and prices, but state outlets (The Herald, ZBC, The Chronicle) could not be fetched except one Herald page, so the government's own account of the economy and foreign ties is thin.
CITE, Heart and Soul, Alpha Media Holdings titles and Daily Maverick were searched but no page from them was opened, so none is cited.

No Crisis Group, ACLED or Chatham House page on 2026 Zimbabwe was opened. The Standard piece on succession says observers spoke to Crisis Group, but it is not attributed to Crisis Group and is cited as a local source.

The Afrobarometer October 2026 findings come from New Zimbabwe without the survey date or sample; the Afrobarometer release itself was not opened. The 79 percent term-limit figure is from 2024 and predates the amendment.
The IMF programme approval date differs between IMF pages (16 April press release and a July reference to March 2026) and was not reconciled.
The lithium rules are unclear: a 25 February suspension of concentrate exports and a June statement that a concentrate ban starts in January 2027 were not reconciled.
The outcome of the Mnangagwa and Putin talks in Moscow in October 2026 was not found, and the Herald page on the May 2025 meeting carries no printed date.
The positions of the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, SADC and the African Union on the amendment were not found; NewsDay mentions calls for sanctions without naming who made them.
The Madzikatidze case outcome, the Constitutional Court ruling on the 2026 challenges and the total external debt figure were not found.
No podcast or documentary on Zimbabwe was verified. Reporter entries rest on single bylines or quotes and were not checked against a wider profile.
